body.text: Recently, reports are once again claiming that Chinese companies have been selling dual-use components to the Houthis to build missiles. Beijing’s motive, these reports argue, is to pressure the United States while leaving no fingerprint that could be traced back to it.

Chinese diplomats have dismissed the claims as baseless allegations, arguing that China maintains strict control on exports and complies with the U.N.-mandated arms embargo. Even if the claims turn out to be true, they said, China is more than willing to investigate and crack down on any violations.

Yet there is a grain of truth to those reports. As technology advances, building missiles is no longer “rocket science,” as the saying goes – the barrier to entry has fallen sharply. Know-how once reserved for a handful of countries is now widely available, allowing a growing number of state and non-state actors to build their own missiles using commercially available components.

It is entirely plausible, then, that Chinese-made components could have found their way into Houthi missiles. It’s unsurprising, even, given that China is often dubbed the “factory of the world” and the growing difficulty of tracking where exports ultimately end up.

That fact alone, however, does not prove that Beijing has greenlit the sales. The more useful question, then, is not whether Chinese-made components are found in Houthi missiles, but whether their presence reflects deliberate Chinese policy.
No Sense in Biting the Hand That Feeds

The Houthis, a militant group fighting for control of Yemen, have recently stepped up their attacks on Saudi oil facilities and sought to close off the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Saudi ships. For Beijing, deliberately sending dual-use components to the Houthis for use toward those ends would be nothing short of shooting itself in the foot. After all, Saudi Arabia is China’s second-largest crude oil supplier, accounting for 14 percent of China’s total imports in 2025.

That relationship held up even after the outbreak of the Hormuz Crisis, which saw many Gulf states’ oil exports plummet due to the Iranian blockade. Saudi Arabia, for its part, was largely able to bypass the Strait of Hormuz – transporting oil through the East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea and shipping it out via the Bab al-Mandab Strait. This route allowed it to export more than 70 percent of its pre-war total crude exports – that is, until the Houthis closed off the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Saudi ships.

That closure has since forced Saudi Arabia to use the Strait of Hormuz and the Suez Canal, neither of which is ideal. Although transit through the Strait of Hormuz has now resumed under U.S. naval escort – with crude, gas, and refined products transiting the strait at up to 81 percent of the pre-war volume – ships attacked by Iran along the way still make headlines. The Suez Canal, meanwhile, is off-limits to fully laden very large crude carriers, and that forces Saudi oil tankers to detour around Africa to reach China – driving up both cost and time.

The Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities, together with the Houthi blockade of Saudi ships, have dealt a heavy blow to China’s energy security. Oil prices in China climbed to a record high this September while a temporary suspension of fuel exports was declared this October.

Moreover, Saudi Arabia is China’s biggest weapons customer in the Middle East, accounting for 45 percent of China’s total regional sales between 2016 and 2025 – with some Chinese-made weapons even being used against the Houthis in recent weeks. For Beijing, deliberately arming the Houthis would not only be ironic but would also risk damaging ties with its biggest regional weapons customer.
The Houthis Are Not Worth the China-U.S. Détente

Managing the China-U.S. geopolitical rivalry – often dubbed the “new cold war” – has been Beijing’s overriding priority this year. While China-U.S. relations remain tense beneath the surface, they have thawed at the surface level, following two high-profile summits between the two countries’ leaders.

Unwilling to risk that hard-won détente, Beijing has largely kept Iran – its comprehensive strategic partner – at arm’s length following the outbreak of the U.S. war on Iran. At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan this September, for example, both the Chinese and Iranian leaders were present yet held no formal meeting.

More tellingly, China has refrained from arming Iran. Even U.S. President Donald Trump himself admitted as much, reiterating this October that he does not believe Beijing is assisting Iran – claiming that he would know if it were. Trump argued that Beijing has too much to lose to take the risk of supplying Iran with materiel.
If Beijing will not arm Iran, it is even less inclined to arm the Houthis, an Iranian-backed non-state actor.
No Weapons Deal Needed for Safe Passage

This is not the first time that Beijing has been accused of arming the Houthis. In 2024, two Chinese companies were sanctioned by the United States for allegedly sending the group dual-use components for use in manufacturing missiles and drones.
Last year, a U.S. think tank went a step further, claiming that Beijing is arming the Houthis in exchange for safe passage for Chinese ships through the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

This year, claims that Beijing has cut a deal with the Houthis resurfaced, following a report that Chinese officials held direct talks with the Iranian-backed group this July to secure safe passage for Chinese ships transiting the Bab al-Mandab Strait; Beijing neither confirmed nor denied the report. Four Chinese ships, however, later transited the strait unscathed, lending the claim weight. A senior Iranian official confirmed that China was “one of the first countries to directly contact the Houthis” regarding transit through Bab al-Mandab Strait.

Although this shows that Beijing has a direct channel of communication to the Houthis, it falls well short of proving that Beijing has agreed to provide weapons components in exchange for passage. In fact, M such a deal is unnecessary.

The Houthis already have an interest in granting Chinese ships safe passage through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, independent of any weapons deal. During the previous Red Sea crisis, the group declared that they would only attack U.S., Israeli, and British ships. In practice, it attacked indiscriminately. This time, however, the Houthis have confined the blockade to Saudi ships alone and even pledged to grant U.S. ships safe passage through the Bab al-Mandab Strait provided the United States stays out of the fight.

It follows, then, that the Houthis have no interest in barring Chinese ships from transiting the strait, either, as doing so would needlessly turn a superpower against the group. Meanwhile, of the four Chinese ships that transited the Bab al-Mandab Strait in July, two diverted from their course – suggesting that Beijing does not have complete faith in the Houthis.
Beijing Should Tighten End-User Controls

Although China can reject the claims that it is deliberately arming the Houthis, Beijing does have a poor track record of tracking where its exports ultimately end up. Chinese-made weapons sold to the UAE, for example, have previously turned up in the hands of the notorious Sudanese Rapid Support Forces despite nominal restrictions on sales to countries in active internal conflict

If Beijing wants fewer fingers pointing at it, it needs tighter end-user controls. “Made in China” is not the same as “sent by Beijing,” but when end-user controls are weak, that distinction collapses in public perception.
